fullText:
Dmitri Dolgov of @Waymo on how to tell if you’re one year away from shipping or ten:

"One pattern that I've seen over and over again is do you have convergence of discovery? The problems that you are seeing today, how different are they from the problems you saw six months ago?"

"As you're pushing on the system, does it feel like you have stability, and you're just iteratively improving your metrics in the same areas?"

"Or does it feel like every six months the landscape is shifting from under you and the problems of today are very different from what you saw a while ago?

"If you don't have that stability, then that's often a good indicator that you got some ways to go."

"If you think you're six months or a year away from deployment, do you have a scorecard that if it were green today would allow you to deploy with confidence?"

"If you don't have one, you're saving that for later, often that turns out to be more difficult than you expected, and there's a long distance to go."

"But if you already have one and you're seeing stability in your discovery and stability in your metrics, and it's just a matter of closing the gap, that is a really good indicator that you're getting pretty close."

@dmitri_dolgov w/ South Park Commons

fullText:
Airbnb's Brian Chesky on the classic management philosophy, and why he rejects it:

"Go through the list of great CEOs, almost none of them that I'm aware of do recurring one-on-ones... Jensen Huang does not do recurring one-on-ones, famously."

"I do think a CEO should meet one-on-one with your people. I don't think it should be recurring... If you wanna get time with me, get a meeting with me. If you wanna call me, call me. Bump into me, talk to me. But most of my recurring meetings are group meetings."

"If there's lots of one-way kinda sensitive topics, there's probably something wrong in the company... If we're having all these sensitive conversations, well, why are they so sensitive? Why can't other people hear about them?"

"If I have a one-on-one with you and you tell me there's a problem and we debate it and we say, 'Here's the solution,' we haven't consulted anyone else. So now we just made a decision and no one else helped, consulted, or knew how we made that decision."

"'Hire great people, trust them, let them do their job, stay out of the details, do recurring one-on-ones.' I don't believe any of that, and I wanna acknowledge that many great leaders do."

@bchesky w/ @sampjacobs

fullText:
Great paper from Meta Superintelligence Labs on compounding inference for long-horizon agents.

One clear approach that's working with large multi-agent systems is persistent memory.

Meta researchers describe a concrete approach for this in this paper.

You'll find that inference-time compute usually goes to separate attempts, so most runs ignore partial work and failed ideas.

Here is how they solve this problem:

GitSwarm gives hundreds of asynchronous agents one shared Git repository.

Each contribution is a commit that records which earlier commits, on any branch, it builds on. There is no central planner. Each worker decides whether to explore, verify, refine, or combine existing work.

With GPT-5.5 Codex workers, it solves all 30 IMOProofBench-Advanced problems in one run. On ProgramBench, it scores 79.4%, against 65.1% for a single Codex agent prompted to keep going at a similar budget.

Score keeps rising with more workers, from 73.1% at 100 to 79.4% at 500. Later workers build on 94.7% of published contributions, and 70.1% of failed research commits are cited by later accepted work.

Paper: https://t.co/5HrLQncE8v

fullText:
Outlier Detection in Python — https://t.co/z6ZME1Vahj from @ManningBooks
———
#Statistics #DataScientist #Analytics #DataScience
———
I have always appreciated the unusual, unexpected, and surprising in science and in data. As famous science author Arthur C. Clarke once said, “The most exciting phrase to hear in science, the one that heralds new discoveries, is not ‘Eureka!’ (I found it) but ‘That’s funny!’” This is the primary reason that I motivated most of the doctoral students that I mentored at GMU to work on some variation of Novelty Discovery (or Surprise Discovery) for their Ph.D. dissertations.

“Surprise discovery” for me is a much more positive, exciting phrase than “outlier detection” or “anomaly detection”, and it is much richer in meaning, in algorithms, and in new opportunities. Finding the surprising unexpected thing in your data is what inspires our exclamation “That’s funny!”, which may be signaling a great discovery (either about your data’s quality, or about your data pipeline’s deficiencies, or about some wholly new scientific concept = SURPRISE DISCOVERY!). As famous astronomer Vera Rubin said, “Science progresses best when new observations (data) force us to alter our preconceptions.”

fullText:
Nice paper on agent memory.

It explores an effective routing mechanism for memory in agents.

The overall finding is that you want a separate retrieval strategy for each type of memory instead of one embedding search over everything.

The authors prove that any single retrieval strategy has an upper bound on expected precision when the memory store holds several types.

MemoType classifies each memory and each query by type, retrieves memories that match the query type, and applies the strategy for that type. A new dataset, TriMEM, provides the type labels needed to train the classifier.

Recall@1 improves by up to 16.18% across three datasets.

Paper: https://t.co/WFiGbPsaLe

fullText:
Pay close attention to custom harnesses.

This is a super interesting paper showing the impact of training inside the harness.

Qwen3-14B goes from 22.2% to 54.8% on Spider 2.0-SQLite when it is trained in the same execution harness it uses at deployment.

Text-to-SQL models are usually trained to write one static query. Deployed database agents inspect schemas, run probe queries and revise, and the harness for that only appears at inference time.

HarnessSQL builds isolated executable databases with hidden answer checks. Teachers run inside the target harness; we keep only verified trajectories for SFT, then apply execution-reward RL.

In addition, Qwen3-8B rises from 15.5% to 45.2%, and both models transfer to BIRD-Interact and LiveSQLBench.

fullText:
As a former math professor and still sometime math researcher, I am rather disappointed in the reaction of the "official math community" to LLMs doing math epically well...

The official hierarchy of award-winning mathematicians and prize committees do not f**king own mathematics, and nobody should have to get permission to prove f**king math theorems !!!  Come on people !!

What would piss me off would be if rich companies were proving important, useful math and keeping it secret and not sharing it with the world (which after all supplied their models with all that critical data on the historical math already created etc.) -- but this is NOT what is happening, at least not so far at least...

LLMs are currently superhuman mathematicians in some respects, yet inferior to strong human mathematicians in other respects.   Whether creative mathematical conjecturing turns out to be AGI-hard is not 100% clear, but I suspect that in some respects the answer will turn out to be yes.

As Josef Urban , a longtime leader of the academic AI theorem-proving world put it very concisely: Math has two big functions, it's fun and it's useful.   

The utility of math should vastly increase as we develop better and better AI-math tools.  And yes, we want to be careful this utility is not captured in a few companies, but this particular problem is not happening now... probably largely because the economic value of new math is relatively indirect compared to a lot of other things.

The fun of doing math will not go away any more than the fun of playing guitar solos goes away if there are robots that can shred faster than any human. The kinds of fun we can most naturally have will shift, as has happened over and over throughout history.

If fancy math prizes or math PhD degrees become infeasible or have to change dramatically, so be it, these were never really the core of math which existed before any of these (in some ways already problematic) social institutions...

I remember when I was an academic mathematician, there was a strong vibe that the mathematicians were at the top of the intellectual hierarchy, with physicists just below, then chemists and engineers, then biologists .. and everyone else just barely above the chimpanzees and politicians.... (The physicists also placed themselves at the top, I think, and mostly considered the mathematicians useful but a bit pedantic and misguided, fussing about missing proof details in calculations that had already been successfully compared to experimental data...) -- 

What we are seeing now I think is the wounding of this sort of overweening math ego...  Plus some practical worry about the potential end of "math researcher" as an economically viable profession -- although current tenured profs are probably safe for a while, as governments and universities are unlikely to adapt to exponential change too much till post-Singularity..

Anyway all this is a sideshow to lots of other related major issues/conflicts unfolding concurrently, it's just one that happens to hit close to home as math was where I started my career..

I have been playing with using LLMs and AI agents to try to invent new kinds of math more appropriate for modeling the experiences of agent hives... a different kind of fun. For those curious...

1) Basics of new "distinction calculus" math

https://t.co/0MvYyYrRys|

2) Attempted start of application to beneficial superintelligence,

https://t.co/TJbGw8Wwhx

Soon enough the agents may not need my help with this sort of thing, in which case I will move on to some alternate method of filling spare late evenings ;)

Figma's Dylan Field says our definition of "slop" keeps silently moving:

"I said, 'AI will lower the floor and raise the ceiling.' And I had to correct myself, because actually that's not what we're seeing yet."

"We're seeing it lower the floor. It's more democratized to do something. But the ceiling doesn't seem to have changed."

"Anything you can verify, AI's great at. Math being number one, maybe cybersecurity number two... You get five designers in a room, they can't agree all the time on exactly what they should do. And that's what's interesting about design. There is not one solution."

"A lot of the stuff that we call slop wouldn't be stuff we'd call slop a month ago or two months ago. As the models change, our definition of slop changes."

"The craft that you imbue into something is reflective of your thinking. It's reflective of your care. People pick up on it. Whether they can articulate it or not, they can tell."

"It creates a lower bound that you have to exceed, but it doesn't define the upper bound. You define the ceiling."
